failures.evidence: Every one is the same shape: `expected: <2026-09-10T00:52:30.482531651Z> but was: <...482532Z>` (LinkExpiryTest.java:190,213,249,284,343,370). Expected comes from the POST /links response, actual from a later GET of the same, unmodified link (each patch was refused 400/401/404, so nothing changed). LinkService.create (LinkService.java:81-104) builds the response from the in-memory entity and `Instant.now()` with no re-read, while V1__initial_schema.sql:32-33 declares `created_at`/`expires_at` as `TIMESTAMP(6) WITH TIME ZONE`; no `truncatedTo` exists anywhere in src/main except JwtSessionService.java:80. So the create response reports nanoseconds the database cannot hold and the GET reports the rounded value. openapi.yaml:67 only says 'Timestamps are ISO-8601 instants in UTC' — it is silent on precision, but no reading of it permits two reads of one immutable field to disagree. Only the implementer can truncate before responding; the tests cannot be relaxed without abandoning 'nothing changed'.

Same defect, different class: `assertEquals(created.createdAt(), fetched.createdAt())` and the expiresAt equivalent at LinkPerformanceTest.java:48-49 fail with `2026-08-11T00:52:46.505809514Z` vs `...505810Z`. The clickCount assertion in the same assertAll passed, so only the two timestamps differ — consistent with the create-response/persisted-value precision mismatch and nothing else. Contract behaviour B (AC7) requires the owner be shown the link's times; it does not license two different answers.

'clicks counted before the outage must survive it: 3 became 0' (DegradedDependencyTest.java:172-175). The test used the contract's own sanctioned mechanism — harness item: 'TestInfrastructure.withCounterTierUnavailable(body) pauses the Redis container through the Docker API and unpauses it in a finally block' — and asserts the contract verbatim: clicks during the outage may be lost, 'but nothing counted either side of it is' (AC20, AC3). Crucially the third assertion, `assertEquals(4, afterRecovery - onRecovery)`, PASSED with onRecovery=0, so the post-recovery total is exactly 4: the three pre-outage clicks are permanently gone, which rules out a transient reconnect read as the explanation. The loss is in implementation code: claim_click_deltas.lua HDELs each field before returning, and RedisClickCounter.claim (RedisClickCounter.java:84-90) swallows the timeout and returns Map.of(), so a command whose response was lost during the pause deletes deltas nobody ever writes down. Medium rather than high only because console logs were not retained in surefire output, so I could not confirm the 'Could not claim click deltas' line directly.

Every failure is `{"error":"rate_limited","message":"Too many requests."} ==> expected: <202> but was: <429>` on Bob's first report. Surefire ran AbuseReportRateLimitTest (properties ABUSE_REPORT_LIMIT_KEY=3, 8+6 reports as bob(), AbuseReportRateLimitTest.java:28-30,48-57,82-94) and finished 1.3s before AbuseReportTest started (report file mtimes 1786409378.49 -> 1786409379.77), leaving Bob's bucket at zero. Buckets are keyed `prefix:bucket:<key>` with no capacity component (RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter.java:74-75), so the drained key survives the context switch; at the 60/min default it refills 1 token/sec, which is why exactly one AbuseReportTest report got its 202 rather than all of them failing. The implementation matches the contract's table (openapi.yaml: abuse-report bucket 'Keyed by customer id' — AbuseReportController.java:44 uses requireByCustomer). The contract anticipates this exact hazard (harness: 'One Redis is shared by every context in the JVM, so buckets outlive a context: resetSharedTierState() flushes it'), but AbuseReportTest declares no @BeforeEach reset and asserts nothing about throttling — it depends on bucket state it never established. Repairable only in author-tests (reset here, or in the drainer's @AfterEach); the 'do not reset in a counting test' caveat is not violated by a reset that precedes the clicks.

`NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "s" is null` at ApiClient.encode(ApiClient.java:315) via getLink/click, plus `LinkPage.items() is null`. Root cause is the same bucket bleed: SignInRateLimitTest (SIGN_IN_LIMIT_KEY=3, ten deliberate guesses, sign-in keyed by client IP per the openapi rate-limit table) finished 0.03s before TenantIsolationTest, whose whole class then ran in 0.032s — no time for the 60/min refill. ApiClient.signInFor (ApiClient.java:134-136) parses whatever body came back into SignInResponse without checking status, so a 429 yields accessToken=null and every later call is unauthenticated, producing null codes and null page items. Not a serialisation defect: ListLinksTest exercises the same LinkPage and passes 7/7. TenantIsolationTest establishes no bucket state and asserts nothing about rate limiting; the fix (reset, or a status check in ApiClient) is in src/test/**, which the implementer is denied by sdlc.yaml:264.

Errors, not failures — the app never boots: `flywayInitializer ... Unable to obtain connection from database: Connection to localhost:5432 refused` at AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.start(AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.java:112) / bootApplication(:51). localhost:5432 is not where the Testcontainers Postgres is; the harness passes the real coordinates via `new SpringApplicationBuilder(...).properties(TestInfrastructure.springProperties())`, and SpringApplicationBuilder.properties() populates Boot's defaultProperties — the lowest-precedence source, below application.yml, whose `spring.datasource.url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shortener}` therefore wins. The corroborating tell is that `server.port=0` is overridden the same way by `server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8080}`. application.yml is frozen design content (present verbatim in c557a64, untouched by the implement diff) and is listed in sdlc.yaml:56 protected_paths, so it is not the implementer's to change; the harness must pass these as command-line args or system properties instead. Fix lives in src/test/**.
failures.test: DurabilityAcrossRestartTest (all 4 methods: aLinkSurvivesARestartAndKeepsRedirecting, aClickCountSurvivesARestart, clicksAfterARestartAddToTheRetainedTotal, aDeletedLinkStaysDownAcrossARestart)

failures.evidence: The test asserts `assertEquals(postOnALiveCode.body(), postOnAnUnissuedCode.body())` (RedirectTest.java:336,339). The actual bodies are Spring's default error JSON — `{"timestamp":"2026-08-11T00:52:54.822+00:00","status":405,"error":"Method Not Allowed","path":"/PYh3WBfFgwutQEkrzO7CGo"}` — which differ in `timestamp` (5ms apart) and in `path` (which echoes the requested code), so the assertion is unsatisfiable against a dispatcher 405 and would fail even for two calls to the same path; neither differing field actually discloses whether a code exists. Two frozen documents disagree: openapi.yaml:47 'Every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape. The catalogue is closed' plus test-contract behaviour B106 'refused identically whether or not the code resolves', versus openapi.yaml note 2 'Every other method on /{code} answers 405 from Spring's own dispatcher. No operation is declared for them' — which the implementation followed. The closed catalogue contains no 405/method_not_allowed code, so ApiError cannot be produced for this status without inventing one, and the contract never states what the 405 body is. Both readings are defensible; a human decides whether the dispatcher 405 is exempt from the ApiError rule, or 'identically' means status-only.

summary:
23 failing methods across 7 classes, plus a coverage_floor gate failure that is purely downstream (no JaCoCo report is produced when the test phase dies). This is the same failure set as the previous round: the implementation has not changed since 23f0d0d — every implement repair attempt failed and the only source change since was ShortCodeUnguessabilityTest — so the earlier split still stands, re-derived from the current reports rather than copied.

IMPLEMENTATION (8 methods). Create/patch responses report timestamps at nanosecond precision while a later GET reads them back from Postgres TIMESTAMP(6) at microsecond precision, so two API reads of one unchanged field disagree (LinkExpiryTest x6, LinkPerformanceTest x1); LinkService builds its response from the in-memory entity with no truncation and no re-read. Separately, DegradedDependencyTest sees a reported click count fall 3 -> 0 across a sanctioned Redis pause, which AC3/AC20 forbid — and the sibling assertion `afterRecovery - onRecovery == 4` passed, so the clicks are genuinely gone rather than momentarily unreadable. The destructive HDEL in claim_click_deltas.lua paired with the timeout-swallowing RedisClickCounter.claim is implementation code either way.

TEST (14 methods). AbuseReportTest and TenantIsolationTest fail entirely on 429s: Surefire runs classes alphabetically, each is preceded by a rate-limit class that drains a shared Redis bucket keyed by the same identity, and neither victim establishes or resets bucket state. Bucket keys carry no capacity component, so the drained key crosses the context boundary. DurabilityAcrossRestartTest errors before it runs at all — its harness passes container coordinates through SpringApplicationBuilder.properties(), i.e. defaultProperties, which lose to the frozen, protected application.yml, so it boots against localhost:5432. None of this is reachable from src/main/**.

CONTRACT (1 method). RedirectTest's byte-equality assertion on the 405 body is unsatisfiable given openapi note 2 ('405 from Spring's own dispatcher'), yet is what the closed-catalogue ApiError rule and behaviour B106 ('refused identically') read as demanding. A human picks which sentence governs.

If I am wrong, the likeliest place is DegradedDependencyTest: surefire did not retain the service log, so I inferred permanent loss from the arithmetic rather than seeing 'Could not claim click deltas'. Re-run that class alone with console output captured before spending the implement attempt on it. The second place to check is the abuse/tenant 429s: if a run with those two classes executed in isolation still 429s, my class-ordering explanation is wrong and the limiter itself is at fault.
